stem: Which development at the global level was under way when India became independent in 1947?
options: The Cold War was beginning and two rival camps were forming
The Cold War had ended and one superpower dominated the world
European colonial empires were expanding across Asia and Africa
The League of Nations was being founded after the First World War
explanation: Correct option: (A). The chapter notes that when India began framing its foreign policy, the Cold War was just beginning and the world was getting divided into two camps led by the US and the USSR. The Cold War ended only around 1990-91, colonialism was collapsing (not expanding) after 1945, and the League of Nations belongs to the period after the First World War; in 1945 the United Nations was being set up.

explanation: Correct option: (C). The chapter says the nuclear programme, a significant part of Nehru's industrialisation plans, was initiated in the late 1940s under the guidance of Homi J. Bhabha. Vikram Sarabhai is associated with the space programme, C.V. Raman with physics research (the Raman effect), and A.P.J. Abdul Kalam with later missile development.

stem: Why has India refused to sign the Nuclear Non-proliferation Treaty (NPT) of 1968?
options: It holds that the NPT is too weak, as it lets every state test freely
It sees the NPT as discriminatory, keeping a monopoly for five powers
Signing the NPT would have forced India to leave the United Nations
The NPT was drafted only after India had built its own nuclear arms
explanation: Correct option: (B). India has always considered the NPT discriminatory, because it applied selectively to non-nuclear states and legitimised the monopoly of the five nuclear weapon powers (the US, USSR, UK, France and China). The NPT restricts, not frees, testing; signing it has nothing to do with UN membership; and India's first test (1974) came after the NPT (1968).

stem: The Janata Party government that came to power in 1977 announced that it would follow 'genuine non-alignment'. What did this imply?
options: That the pro-Soviet tilt in foreign policy would be corrected
That India would leave the Non-Aligned Movement altogether
That India would join the US-led military alliance system
That India would end all its relations with the Soviet Union at once
explanation: Correct option: (A). The chapter explains that 'genuine non-alignment' implied correcting the pro-Soviet tilt in foreign policy; since then all governments have sought better relations with China and close ties with the US. It did not mean leaving NAM, joining a US-led military alliance or ending ties with the Soviet Union, which remained an important friend.

stem:
Assertion (A): Even in the decade 1962-1971, when India faced three wars, foreign policy played only a limited role in party politics.
Reason (R): Indian politics is marked by broad agreement among parties on national integration, protection of international boundaries and questions of national interest.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (A). Both statements are true. The chapter draws A as a conclusion from R: because parties broadly agree on national integration, international boundaries and the national interest, differences on how to conduct external relations remain minor, so foreign policy plays only a limited role in party politics. Hence R correctly explains A.
